# Running tests

**track**
: One of the five JVMs of `ant testFast`.

**shard**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.

**code state**
: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.

## The two suites

`ant testFast` runs about 2,560 tests in five tracks, four at once, in about 5 to 7 minutes:

- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes, except `OneLibraryJUTest`.
- onelibrary: `OneLibraryJUTest` over `one_library_tests/`, with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. It starts when another track ends.

`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 680 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.

`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.

The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:

    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'

The two suites work in the same way:

- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.

To run a suite:

- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.

## The switches that the harness reads

Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.

- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.

## Outside the gate

- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
- No suite and no stage of the gate runs the team demos, the programs of `ProjectFortress/demos/`. Keep each of the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reaching its end (P-79). Check them with the demo driver below, not with `ant testDemos`, whose test of the output is weaker:
  - If your change edits walk, the parser, a phase that both paths run, a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`interpreter.md`, "Natives") or the interpreter's library, run the driver once, after your last edit of code.
  - Print the driver with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md#Commands worked out'`. Save the first script that it prints, under "The demo driver", without the text around it, as `tmp/run-demos.sh` in your tree.
  - From the tree's root, after you set up the call, run `bash tmp/run-demos.sh tmp/demos`. It runs long, so run it in the background with a log (`session.md`, "Long commands"). It runs the demos under walk one at a time and writes `tmp/demos/summary.tsv`.
  - The driver's last line of output, before the log's `EXIT=` line, must read 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. A demo reaches its end if it exits 0 and its output holds no "fail" in upper or lower case.
  - If your change breaks a demo and you know how to repair the demo, repair it in the commit of your change. Otherwise, report the demo, its output and the ledger row that holds the missing feature, as a defect that your change makes or uncovers.
- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).

## When to run a whole suite

- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk, of a phase that both paths share or of such a class under `nativeHelpers/`, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`), the parser or such a class, run both.
- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the runtime (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below, and the demos where "Outside the gate" asks for them. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests.

The suites do not check these:

- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
- the linker's aliasing of apis;
- `fortress unparse`;
- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.

If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.

## One test, or a few

Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.

### Interpreter tests

Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:

    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]

- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.

To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss

The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").

### Compiled tests

Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`). The tests of `one_library_tests/` compile against the one library: run them with `ant testOneLibrary`.

The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.

    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1

- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.

To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test

Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.

## One unit-test class, or one track

To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.

To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:

- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.
- `ant testOneLibrary`: the onelibrary track.

# The Claude Code session: the Bash tool, long commands, waits and stops

**prompt cache**
: API's copy of a conversation's context. It lives five minutes for an agent and one hour for the main session. Each request to the API within that time reads the cache and renews it. The first request after a longer wait writes the whole context again: late in a long task, hundreds of thousands of tokens.

**interrupt**
: Stop of the session's turn, by the stop button. It kills every agent that runs in the background at that moment, of the Agent tool or of a Workflow.

**stop of the process**
: End of the session's Claude Code process. It kills every agent. It keeps the conversation, the transcripts and the disk: worktrees, uncommitted edits and logs. A command started with `nohup` (below) survives a stop, but not a restart of the machine.

**automatic permission check**
: Check that approves each tool call in auto mode. It can refuse a call, also a call that the curator approved in chat.

## The Bash tool and waits

The Bash tool stops a call at 120 s, unless the call passes a longer `timeout`, at most 600 s. It kills the command, or moves it to the background. It also refuses a command that starts with `sleep N` and goes on to another command, such as `sleep 60; tail build.log`. Wait with `wait_for` instead (below).

- In an agent, keep every wait under 240 s.
- In the main session, keep every wait under an hour. The main session can also watch a run with the `Monitor` tool.

## Long commands

If a command can take more than a minute or two, start it detached with `nohup`, after the setup lines, whose exports it inherits. Write the command and the log in the line itself:

    nohup bash -c '( ant compileAll ) > tmp/build.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/build.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &

Keep the setup lines and the `nohup` line as separate lines. `A && nohup B &` runs `A` in the background too, so its `cd` and its exports do not reach the lines after it in the same call.

The log gets the output, then a last line `EXIT=<status>`. The automatic permission check refuses a shell function that passes the command to `bash -c` in a variable, because it cannot read the command.

The shell function `wait_for` waits for the `EXIT=` line, for 240 s at most. If the line is there, it prints the log's verdict lines and returns 0: ant's `BUILD` and `Total time:`, JUnit's `OK (`, `FAILURES!!!` and `Tests run:`, and `EXIT=`. If not, it returns 1.

Run `wait_for` until it returns 0, each time in a new Bash call. Give that call a `timeout` above 240 s, such as 300000 ms: the timeout only guards the call, and `wait_for` itself returns by 240 s. Define the function in each call that uses it. Grep the log for the lines that you need.

    wait_for () {    # wait_for <logfile> [max seconds, at most 240]; call again until it returns 0
        local n=0 max=${2:-240}
        case "$max" in ''|*[!0-9]*) max=240 ;; esac ; [ "$max" -gt 240 ] && max=240
        while ! grep -q '^EXIT=' "$1" 2>/dev/null ; do
            sleep 5 ; n=$((n+5))
            [ "$n" -ge "$max" ] && { echo "still running after ${n}s" ; return 1 ; }
        done
        grep -n '^BUILD \|^Total time:\|^OK (\|^FAILURES!!!\|^Tests run:\|^EXIT=' "$1"
    }

If your brief says that you run beside a batch, a run of other agents that build and test at the same time, run every build, suite, stage and program under `nice -n 19`, after `nohup`. Run one command of your own at a time that starts a JVM. The JVMs that it starts count with it.

- Start such a command only when the `available` column of `free -g` shows 6 GB or more. If it shows less, check again in each call of a wait, as `wait_for` waits, for at most 30 minutes. If it still shows less, start nothing and report back.
- A timed run of the checker is a plain run, under the rules for every other run here; it takes no lock and waits for no other work.

## Stopping processes

Stop only the processes that run under your tree's path. To find a process's path, read `readlink /proc/<pid>/cwd`, or the paths in its arguments.

Kill by process id, with `kill <pid>`. A pattern, as in `pkill -f`, also matches other agents' copies of the same scripts, and your own call's shell, which it then kills.

## After an interrupt or a stop of the process

If your work starts again after an interrupt or a stop of the process:

1. Read what is on disk first: `git log` and `git status` in your tree, and your logs.
2. If a step's log has ended and the tree has not changed since, the step is done. A log has ended if it has its `EXIT=` line, or its verdict or table is complete.
3. If a log has no `EXIT=` line yet, its command may still run. Look for its process under your tree's path. If it runs, wait for it with `wait_for`.
4. Continue at the first step whose log is missing, cut off or failed.

## When the automatic permission check refuses a call

- Do not try for the same result with another tool, by another route or in a later turn.
- Report the refusal and what was not done because of it. The way through is the curator's: manual approval for the session, or an allow rule for the command (`/permissions`).

# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- A probe is a task of a brief that builds a change to answer a question and does not land it. Commit its change as a patch file, with its report and programs, in the `probes/` folder that the brief names, and no edit of the original tree. If the brief names no folder, commit nothing of the probe: give the patch's path and the report in your final message.
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- Do not commit `.claude/worktrees/` or `.claude/agents/`, which show as untracked in a fresh clone.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, also gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree leaves its branch. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:

         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable

     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The platform rebuilds a lost container from `blinded-fable`.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.

# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

1	# The compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime
2	
3	**count stage**
4	: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library, on the `FortressLibrary` component and the apis that it imports, and prints the errors in a table: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total is the checker count.
5	
6	**distance stage**
7	: Stage of the gate that runs the compiled checker over fourteen components of the interpreter's library, `FortressLibrary` among them, runs each of the checker's steps on each component whatever the earlier steps report, and prints the errors in a table. Your brief gives its command when you need it.
8	
9	The code of this area is in these directories:
10	
11	- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
12	- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
13	- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.
14	
15	The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.
16	
17	## What the two paths share
18	
19	After the phases, each path has its own code for these:
20	
21	- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
22	- Number natives: walk's glue classes, in `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`ZZ32.java`, `ZZ64.java`).
23	- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
24	- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.
25	
26	Both paths run the helpers, the public static methods of classes under `nativeHelpers/`.
27	
28	The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.
29	
30	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
31	
32	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, it uses the one library in their place. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.
33	
34	Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: the switch-over deletes them, and their tests stay. Two exceptions (P-37): its numeral types and coercions follow `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", and a brief may ask to declare each built-in number type as one `value object`, the form that both libraries are to take. If a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is wrong, fix the helper's Java, even if the prelude binds it, and leave the prelude's text: its binding gives the fix. Change with it a compiled test that pinned the old result.
35	
36	## What the compiled path cannot compile yet
37	
38	For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:
39	
40	- `spawn`;
41	- an object expression;
42	- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.
43	
44	It compiles a local function as a closure, also one that calls itself or another local function of its block. It refuses these forms (ledger row 304):
45	
46	- a local function with static parameters of its own: 'Can't compile a local function with static parameters of its own yet';
47	- two local functions of one name in a block: 'Can't compile overloaded local functions yet';
48	- a local function with the `atomic` modifier: 'Can't compile a local function with this modifier yet'.
49	
50	A type assumption `e asif T` has the value of `e`, but the call around it chooses its declaration as if `e` were a `T`, a supertype of `e`'s type (`Specification/basic/expressions/type-annotation.tex`). The code generator compiles one at a dotted call's receiver, at a call of a functional method or an overloaded function whose every argument is an assumption, and elsewhere as the value of `e`. It refuses these forms (ledger row 818):
51	
52	- a call of a functional method or an overloaded function with an assumption at some of its arguments but not all: 'Can't compile a dispatched call whose arguments are not all type assumptions';
53	- a generic method on an assumed receiver: 'Can't compile a type assumption at the receiver of a generic method yet';
54	- a call of an overloaded generic function with an assumption at an argument: 'Can't compile a type assumption at a call of an overloaded generic function yet'.
55	
56	It also refuses a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose own header or `extends` entry has a `where` clause, and emits nothing for the clause. A call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, links, but dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 867). `compiler_tests/XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled.test` records it: copy its form for such a call. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private`, `abstract` and `test`, such as `override` (ledger row 650). A trait or object that extends a generic trait compiles with `Any` as the static argument. With `Bottom`, `Self` or an abbreviated type there, the code generator refuses the declaration. An abbreviated type is a short form, such as `RR64[3]` for an array type. With a tuple that holds `Any` there, the code generator crashes (ledger row 889).
57	
58	The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.
59	
60	Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).

62	## What the code generator does
63	
64	- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
65	- It runs a program's own `coerce` from a numeral once for each place where the numeral is written, in the component class's static initializer, except where the place's type names a type parameter (below). The runtime initializes the class of each component that the program's classes name before `run()`, in one task. So a coercion's output comes before the program's first line, and the parallel parts of a coercion's body run one after another there. A coercion that raises stops the program before `run()`. A test of a coercion that raises sets `run_exits_nonzero=true` (`tests-writing.md`).
66	- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
67	- The `value` modifier adds the mark interface `ValueObjectMark` to the object's class. The compiled `SEQV` (`nativeHelpers/equality.java`) reads the mark. The modifier does not inline or unbox the fields.
68	- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet. If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):
69	
70	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'
71	
72	## The runtime
73	
74	- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes, for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417), and to choose a call's opcode from the class file of the called method's class, without loading that class. Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
75	- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`), and an object's `var` field in a cell that the object holds. Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches. From the switch-over, it also tracks each element of the one library's arrays, by array and index: `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java` calls the transaction's methods `TXReadSlot` and `TXWriteSlot`. Walk does not run this class, so test an edit of it with `ArrayStoreJUTest`, beside it.

77	## Natives
78	
79	`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
80	
81	A body `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")` binds one such method, a helper, too. In a compile, at the parse, the compiled path, and not walk, rewrites the body as a call of the method through a generated `import java`, with `self` first in a trait or object (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`). The checker then checks the declaration against the method's Java signature. In a compile, it reads `int` as `ZZ32`, `long` as `ZZ64`, `float` as `RR32`, `double` as `RR64`, `boolean` as `Boolean`, `String` as `JavaString`, `BigInteger` as `ZZ` and `Object` as `Any` (`NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType`). The compile stops in these cases:
82	
83	- If the string is in that package but names no public static method: 'builtinPrimitive names no static helper: …'.
84	- If the string names a glue class or anything else outside that package: 'Variable builtinPrimitive is not defined.'
85	- If the declaration has a varargs parameter: the same message (ledger row 849).
86	- If the declaration is a local function or a method of an object expression: the same message. The rewrite reaches only a component's declarations and the members of its traits and objects (ledger row 865).
87	
88	The rewrite runs only in a JVM that has made a Fortress repository of the compiled path, the compiler's store of components, not this git repository. Walk's repository switches it off again. `fortress compile` makes one, and so do `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` and `typecheck` (`Shell.compilerPhases`). `fortress parse` and `fortress api` make none, so they rewrite a body only after a compile in the same JVM (ledger row 882). Alone, they pass a misspelt helper. Test a binding with `compile`. In a suite, the result of `parse` or `api` depends on whether a compile ran earlier in the same JVM.
89	
90	To test a helper on the compiled path, write a compiled test whose own declarations bind it, as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` does. Until the switch-over, a compiled test cannot reach the interpreter's library's bindings.
91	
92	The count stage and the distance stage check the interpreter's library with the same rewrite. There, the checker differs from a compile in these ways:
93	
94	- A string that names a glue class, or a declaration with a varargs parameter, does not stop the check. The body stays a call of `builtinPrimitive`, typed at the declared result type, and no Java signature checks it (ledger row 849).
95	- The checker reads a helper's Java types as the interpreter's library's types: `String` as `String`, not `JavaString`, and the rest as in a compile.
96	- A component that imports a DSL grammar is parsed by other code (`GraphRepository.syntaxExpand`), which does not rewrite its bindings. So, as for a glue class, no Java signature checks them.
97	- The count stage checks only the `FortressLibrary` component's bindings. A binding of another component, as `FortressBuiltin`'s, only the distance stage checks.
98	
99	The checker, in a compile and in both stages, reads `int` as `NN32` or `Char`, and `long` as `NN64`, only for six transfer helpers with fixed names (`NamingCzar.java:373-384`, `:494-503`). Where a binding gives a parameter, `self` or the result the type `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char`, and the helper has `int` or `long` there, the rewrite passes that value through the matching transfer helper. `self` gets a transfer helper only in a method of one of these three types itself. The transfer helpers return their argument unchanged. So the checker accepts such a binding whatever helper it names, a signed one included, as `simpleIntArith.intLT` for `NN32`'s `<`. If you move a binding over these types onto a helper, test it on both paths at values where a signed and an unsigned reading differ (2^31 and above for `NN32`, 2^63 and above for `NN64`), as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Compiled.fss` and `tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Walk.fss` do. If the class has more than one method of the helper's name and number of parameters, the rewrite adds no transfer helper. The checker then reports 'Could not check call to function builtinPrimitive_<Class>_<method>', followed by '… is not applicable to an argument of type …'.
100	
101	The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method. In the count stage and the distance stage, a type maps only if the interpreter's library declares it. So there, a binding stops its component if any method of its helper's class has a type that only the compiler's prelude declares. The distance stage then counts the component as a stopped target. `nativeHelpers/systemOps` is such a class: its `getArgs` answers `StringVector`, so the message is 'FortressBuiltin.StringVector is undefined.' (F-321). Bind a helper of another class.

103	## Traps of the compiled path
104	
105	- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit. The prelude's `||` takes the string first only, so `c || s` for a `Character` value `c` is refused (ledger row 965). Put a string first, as `("" || c) || s`.
106	- Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares no `=/=` at `RR32` and `RR64`, so the checker refuses `r =/= 0` for an `RR64` value `r` (ledger row 1059). Write `NOT (r = 0)`. At `RR32`, `=` compiles and overflows the stack when it runs (ledger row 528). Bind an `RR32` value `c` at `RR64` first, as `r: RR64 = c`, and compare `r`.
107	- A parameter of a declared tuple type is one JVM parameter for each element (F-378). So in a `VerifyError`, the method's descriptor lists each element of a tuple parameter as a parameter of its own. These three tuple forms fail:
108	  - an object's method overloaded at a pair and at another type fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 1054). Give the two methods two names;
109	  - an object whose one value parameter is a pair dies in its constructor with `ClassCastException` (ledger row 1055). Add a second value parameter beside the pair, as `object Holder(n: ZZ32, var pr: (ZZ32, ZZ32))`;
110	  - a generic operator whose one parameter has its type parameter's type, applied to a pair, dies at the call with `NoSuchMethodError`, as `pr!!` for `opr (x: T)!![\T\] : T = x` and `pr = (1, 2)` (ledger row 1056). Write no such call in a compiled program.
111	- A `try`'s `forbid` clause lists exception types: an exception of a listed type that no `catch` clause took is wrapped in a `ForbiddenException`, which the `try` throws. A `try`'s `finally` clause does not run when one of these leaves the `try` block: an `exit`, an exception that no `catch` clause takes, or the `ForbiddenException` that the `try` throws (ledger row 890). So write no compiled program that relies on `finally` after an exception or an `exit` leaves the `try`. A test that needs it is an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`). A `try` whose block can throw, with a `finally` clause and no `catch` or `forbid` clause, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load (ledger row 891).
112	- To fork is to run as tasks that can run at once. A call's arguments and an operator's operands fork, as the rule says, where two or more of them are calls, written `f(x)`, of functions that the program declares. So write no compiled program that relies on the order in which its arguments are evaluated. Until the switch-over, the calls written in the compiler's prelude do not fork, so a compiled `SUM` runs one body at a time (ledger row 982). A compiled parallel `for` runs its bodies at once: use it in a test of parallelism.
113	- An `atomic` block (`atomic do ... end`) or atomic expression (`atomic e`, as `atomic 1`), a `try` or a `label` block as a call's argument after the first, as `f(k, atomic do ... end)`, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load, unless the arguments fork (ledger row 322). So does a `try` as an operator's operand after the first (ledger row 526). Bind its value in a statement of its own.
114	- Numerals and sizes depart from `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways:
115	  - At a place whose type names a type parameter of its generic declaration, a numeral's coercion runs at each evaluation (ledger row 957). If the body needs the value at one instance only, bind it once, at a top-level variable whose type names no type parameter.
116	  - Until the switch-over, `RR64` converts only an `RR32` and a numeral, and `RR32` only a numeral. So a `ZZ32` value where an `RR64` is expected is refused (ledger row 442). Write `i.asRR64` for a `ZZ32` value `i`.
117	  - At a binding without a declared type, the checker refuses a `try` whose block and `catch` clause end in numerals, as `x = try 4 catch e Exception => 5 end`: 'NaturalNumeral cannot be written in a program except as a parameter's type.' (ledger row 1074). It also refuses a tuple binding to a `case` or a `try` whose branches are numeral tuples, as `(a, b) = case k of 1 => (1, 2) else => (3, 4) end`: 'Right-hand side has type OR(...), but left-hand side is a tuple of 2 variables.' (ledger row 1075). Declare the types, as `(a, b): (ZZ32, ZZ32) = case ...`.
118	  - A numeral with a radix point at a place that fixes no type, which rounds to an infinity at `RR64`, gives `Infinity`, as under walk (ledger row 980). Assert no value for it in a test.
119	  - A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, raises a `java.lang.Error` that no `catch` sees (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
120	  - As a `typecase`'s selector, a numeral keeps its own type, as `NaturalNumeral[\1,10,7\]`, so `typecase 7 of ZZ32 => ...` is refused as unreachable (ledger row 963). Bind the selector to a variable first, as `x = 7`, then write `typecase x of ...`.

120	  - As a `typecase`'s selector, a numeral keeps its own type, as `NaturalNumeral[\1,10,7\]`, so `typecase 7 of ZZ32 => ...` is refused as unreachable (ledger row 963). Bind the selector to a variable first, as `x = 7`, then write `typecase x of ...`.
121	  - A `label` block that ends in a numeral, where an `exit ... with` gives the block a `ZZ32` value, stops the code generator: 'Error trying to close method scope' (ledger row 340). Bind the numeral to a typed variable first, as `none: ZZ32 = -1`, and end the block with the variable.
122	  - At a place that fixes a type (`revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"), the checker refuses an atomic expression whose value is a numeral, as `atomic if c then 1 else 0 end`, and `atomic 1` fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 1043). Write `atomic do ... end`.
123	- An `exit` that runs after its `label` block has completed, from a function made in the block, ends a compiled program with the Java exception `LabelExit`, which no `catch` clause takes. Under walk, a `catch` clause of the library's `LabelException` takes it. The rules do not settle which is right (ledger row 1041).
124	- Where an object overloads an inherited functional method by declarations of its own, and `self` is not the first parameter, the compiled dispatch method tests the receiver's type where it should test the other argument's. A call then dies with `ClassCastException` (ledger row 573). Where the receiver has the parameter type of one of the object's own declarations, the call runs that declaration whatever the argument (ledger row 1038). Put `self` first in such overloads.
125	- On the compiled path, two `value` objects with a `var` field, built alike, are not strictly equivalent: `V(1) === V(1)` is `false` (ledger row 112).
126	- A reference to a generic function with one declaration, as `count[\F extends Object\](b: Box[\F\]): ZZ32`, takes its instance from the arrow type that receives it. Where the receiving type is not an arrow type, as in `p(count)` for `p(x: Any)`, the compile passes and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 1012). Write the static argument there, as `p(count[\ZZ32\])`. The checker refuses a reference to a name with several declarations of which one is generic, unless one without static parameters fits the receiving arrow type (ledger row 1009). Pass a function of one declaration that calls the name.
127	- Where the initialiser of a top-level variable `b` assigns to a top-level `var a`, a compiled read of `a` before the first read of `b` gives the old value (ledger row 1011). Read `b` before you read `a`.
128	- A `typecase` tuple pattern with an untyped binder, as `(x, y: ZZ32)`, stops the code generator: 'typcase match failure!' (ledger row 964). Walk stops on the same clause when it evaluates the `typecase`, with the same message. Give each binder a type.
129	- Where a `typecase` clause types its binder at a trait above the selector's object type, a method call on the binder fails the JVM's verification, as `typecase a of x: Shape => x.nm()` for `a: Sq` and `object Sq extends Shape` (ledger row 1067). Call the method on the selector, as `a.nm()`.
130	- In a `typecase` over a value `x` of a type parameter `X`, as `X extends Shape`, a clause `x': Marked =>` gives its binder `x'` the intersection of `Marked` and `X`. The checker refuses a call on `x'` of a method of `X`'s bound, as `x'.name()` for a method `name` of `Shape` (ledger row 1072). Call it on the selector, as `x.name()`.
131	- In a trait with a `comprises` clause, the checker refuses a getter of a listed type read on `self`: `self.d` in `trait Q comprises { R }`, `d` a field of `R`, gives '(Q & {R}) has no getter called d' (ledger row 1071). Bind `self` at the listed type first, as `r: R = self`, and read `r.d`.
132	- A function expression whose type is an intersection dies when its closure is made. Such a type comes from a call typed by the intersection of its candidates' return types, as `fn () => choose(m)`, where `choose` has declarations at two traits that `m`'s type extends, each with its own return type (`compiler_tests/XXXIntersectionClosureResult.fss`): 'Unable to read serialized data for Intersection??' (ledger row 559). Write none in a compiled program.
133	- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
134	- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
135	- A clean link does not prove that every call has its method. These die at run time with `NoSuchMethodError`:
136	  - a call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815);

140	## The checker's gaps
141	
142	- Overloads: in its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786).
143	- The Return Type Rule: the checker refuses a pair of declarations that the rule accepts: a generic declaration beside one without static parameters whose domain is a tuple of object types, as `ident[\T\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: (Circle, Circle)): (Circle, Circle)`, `Circle` an object (ledger row 1048). Walk loads and runs the pair.
144	- A tie: where two generic candidates fit a call equally, the checker sorts the candidates and keeps the first. The sort's order varies with what the same JVM compiled before. So the call's static type, or a crash, 'V is not in the kind env', can change with the order of the suite (ledger rows 499, 1046, 1047). If a compiled test passes alone and fails in the suite, look for such a tie first.
145	- Inheritance: the checker refuses an object that reaches a generic self-typed trait's method along two paths, one through a trait that declares the method again at the same parameter types: 'There are multiple declarations of m with the same parameter type'. Without static parameters it accepts the form. Walk runs the lower trait's declaration. The specification's section "Method Declarations" (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`) does not settle which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 1037).
146	- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the compiled code does not check it. A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
147	  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
148	  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
149	  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
150	- A reduction without its static argument, whose bound names its parameter, such as `SUM`: the checker reports a type error in its body as the big operator's refusal, 'is not applicable to an argument of type ()' (ledger row 1015). Write the static argument to read the body's error.
151	- Imports: `import A.{...}`, with the three dots written, imports every name of `A`. The overloading check also reads `A`'s declarations of a name that the component imports by name from another api. So `import A.{...}` beside `import B.{ pick }`, where both apis declare `pick(x: P)`, is refused: 'There are multiple declarations of pick' (ledger row 813). Leave the name out of the whole import, as `import A.{...} except { pick }`.
152	- An `except` clause leaves out each identifier that it lists, on both paths. Neither path leaves out an infix operator that it lists. So where a component lists `-` in `except` and declares its own `-` at the api's parameter types, the code generator stops. Walk runs the component's own `-` (ledger row 814).
153	- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
154	- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. Where the variable is a size, a compiled call that passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 307). Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).

156	## The `fortress` commands
157	
158	`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.
159	
160	- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
161	- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
162	- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
163	- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches. With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, `useCompilerLibraries()` points them to the one library (`Shell.java:377-388`).

204	## The checker's time
205	
206	This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.
207	
208	The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 80 to 180 seconds, more under load. It can run past the Bash tool's 120-second limit, so run it in the background (`session.md`). It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.
209	
210	The checker checks every api first, and the component only if no api has an error. In each api or component, it stops at the first of its stages that finds errors. The stages run in this order (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`, `checkCompilationUnit`):
211	
212	1. The type hierarchy and the type check.
213	2. The overloading check, which also compares the overloads' return types.
214	3. In the component only, the export check (`library.md`, "Designing a change").
215	
216	So the count misses the errors of the later stages, and a fix of an early error can raise it.
217	
218	The table's rows tell a clean run from a run that the checker did not finish:
219	
220	- `#total 0` and `#locations 0`: the checker reached the component and found no error.
221	- `#stopped`, in place of `#total` and `#locations`: the errors came from a phase before the checker, such as the parse. The checker reported none and did not reach the component. The script exits 1, and the gate reads the table as red.
222	- `#crash`: the first crash of the overloading check that the run survived, or `none`.
223	
224	If the run printed no error total and was not clean, the script writes no table and exits 1.
225

229	- The two `run.txt` files are equal after you replace each run's own tree path with one word, such as `TREE`. Any difference fails.

- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). There are two exceptions, each so that both paths do the same before the switch-over, and each copy goes with the prelude: the numerals, where the prelude carries the design of P-174 and P-176; and the built-in number types, where it takes the form of P-178. The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.

\seclabel{function-decls}

\begin{Grammar}

\EXP{=} \emph{Expr} \\
&$|$& \emph{FnSig} \\

\emph{FnSig} &::=& \emph{SimpleName} \EXP{\mathrel{\mathtt{:}}} \emph{Type}\\

\emph{FnMods} &::=& \emph{FnMod}$^+$\\

\emph{FnMod} &::=& \emph{AbsFnMod} $|$ \KWD{private}\\

\emph{AbsFnMod} &::=& \emph{LocalFnMod} $|$
\KWD{test}\\

\emph{LocalFnMod} &::=& \KWD{atomic} $|$ \KWD{io}\\

\emph{FnHeaderFront}
&::=& \emph{NamedFnHeaderFront}\\
&$|$& \emph{OpHeaderFront} \\

\emph{NamedFnHeaderFront}
&::=& \emph{Id} \option{\emph{StaticParams}} \emph{ValParam} \\

\emph{ValParam} &::=& \emph{BindId}\\
&$|$& \texttt(\option{\emph{Params}}\texttt)\\

\emph{Params}
&::=&
(\emph{Param}\EXP{,})$^*$ \options{\emph{Varargs}\EXP{,}} \emph{Keyword}(\EXP{,}\emph{Keyword})$^*$\\
&$|$&
(\emph{Param}\EXP{,})$^*$  \emph{Varargs}\\
&$|$& \emph{Param}(\EXP{,} \emph{Param})$^*$\\

\emph{VarargsParam} &::=& \emph{BindId}\EXP{\COLONOP}\emph{Type}\EXP{...} \\

\emph{Varargs} &::=& \emph{VarargsParam}\\

\emph{Keyword} &::=& \emph{Param}\EXP{=}\emph{Expr} \\

\emph{PlainParam} &::=& \emph{BindId} \option{\emph{IsType}} \\
&$|$& \emph{Type} \\

\emph{Param} &::=& \emph{PlainParam}\\

\emph{FnHeaderClause} &::=& \option{\emph{IsType}} \emph{FnClauses} \\

\emph{FnClauses} &::=& \option{\emph{Throws}} \option{\emph{Where}}
\emph{Contract} \\

\emph{Throws} &::=& \KWD{throws} \emph{MayTraitTypes}\\

\end{Grammar}

Syntactically, a function declaration consists of
an optional sequence of modifiers followed by
the name of the function, optional static parameters
(described in \chapref{trait-parameters}),
the value parameter with its (optionally) declared type,
an optional type of a return value,
an optional declaration of thrown checked exceptions
(discussed in \chapref{exceptions}),
an optional \KWD{where} clause (discussed in \secref{where-clauses}),
a contract for the function (discussed in \secref{contracts}),
and finally an optional body expression preceded by the token \EXP{=}.
A \KWD{throws} clause does not include naked type variables.
Every element in a \KWD{throws} clause is a subtype of
\TYP{CheckedException}.
When a function declaration includes a body expression, it is called a
\emph{function definition}.
Function declarations can be mutually recursive.

Function declarations can include the following special modifiers:
\paragraph{\KWD{atomic}:}
A function with the modifier \KWD{atomic} acts as if its entire
body were surrounded in an \KWD{atomic} expression discussed in
\secref{atomic}.

\paragraph{\KWD{io}:}
Functions that perform externally visible input/output actions
are said to be \KWD{io} functions.
An \KWD{io} function must not be invoked from a non-\KWD{io} function.

A function takes exactly one argument, which may be a tuple.
When a function takes a tuple argument, we abuse terminology by saying that
the function takes multiple arguments.
Value parameters cannot be mutated inside the function body.

A function's value parameter consists of a parenthesized,
comma-separated list of bindings where each binding is one of:
\begin{itemize}
\item A plain binding ``\VAR{identifier}''
or ``\EXP{\VAR{identifier}\COLONOP{}T}''
\item A varargs binding ``\EXP{\VAR{identifier}\COLONOP{}T\ldots}''
\item A keyword binding ``\EXP{\VAR{identifier}=\exp}''
or ``\EXP{\VAR{identifier}\COLONOP{}T=\exp}''
\end{itemize}
When the parameter is a single plain binding without a declared type,
enclosing parentheses may be elided.
The following restrictions apply:  No two bindings may have the same
    identifier.
No keyword binding may precede a plain binding.
No varargs binding may follow a keyword binding or precede a plain binding.
Note that it is permitted to have a single plain binding,
or to have no bindings.  The latter case, ``()'', is considered equivalent
to a single plain binding of the ignored identifier ``\_'' of type (), that
is, ``\EXP{(\_\COLONOP())}''.
Also, there can be at most one varargs binding.

A parameter declared by keyword binding is called
a \emph{keyword parameter};
a keyword parameter must be declared with
a \emph{default} expression,
which is used when no argument is bound to the parameter explicitly.
Syntactically, the default expression is specified
after an \EXP{=} sign.
The default expression of a parameter $x$ of function $f$
is evaluated each time the function is called
without a value provided for $x$ at the call site.
All parameters occurring to the left of $x$
are in scope of its default expression.
All parameters following $x$ must include default expressions as well;
$x$ is in scope of their default expressions and the body of the function.
When an argument is passed explicitly for a keyword parameter,
that argument must be passed as a \emph{keyword argument}.
(See \secref{function-app}.)
If no type is declared for a keyword parameter,
the type is inferred from the static type of its default expression.

A parameter declared by varargs binding is called
a \emph{varargs parameter};
it is used to pass a variable number of arguments to a function
as a single heap sequence.
The type of a varargs parameter
    is \EXP{\TYP{HeapSequence}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} where \VAR{T} is
    the type mentioned in (or inferred for) that binding.
\note{See the library section for a discussion of
\TYP{HeapSequence}.}
\revision{revival-varargs}{No library declares \TYP{HeapSequence}, nor the
immutable sequence that the team's draft note at the start of
\secref{function-app} agreed on in its place.
Both implementations give a varargs parameter the array type of \library\ that
the compiled type checker's authors named for it,
\EXP{\TYP{ImmutableArray}\llbracket{}T, \mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket}: the
interpreter binds the parameter to an immutable one-dimensional array of the
arguments, and the compiled type checker types the parameter in the body at
that type.
The compiled path's own library declares no such type, so there the compiled
type checker refuses every use of a varargs parameter, in a body, a contract
or a function expression, naming the type, and the code generator refuses a
function with a varargs parameter, naming it too.
Against \library, the code generator passes the arguments that no plain
binding takes as one such array, which the library's factory makes and the
caller fills in order: at the call, or, where another declaration of the name
takes as many arguments, in the dispatch method's branch for the varargs
declaration.}
Note that the type of a varargs parameter cannot be omitted.
If a function does not have a varargs parameter
then the number of arguments is fixed by the function's type.
Note that a varargs parameter is not allowed to have a default expression.
