\section{Function Applications}
\seclabel{function-app}

\note{varargs arguments (10/30/07)

Is there any reason to use \TYP{HeapSequence} which is mutable to implement varargs tuples?
How about implementing them in terms of some covariant data type?

We agreed to implement varargs tuples using \TYP{ReadOnlyHeapSequence} which is immutable and
invariant. We'll add \TYP{MakeReadOnlyHeapSequence} into the core library.
}

Fortress allows functions to be overloaded; there may be multiple function
declarations with the same function name in a single lexical scope.
Thus, we need to determine which functional declarations are applicable to
a function application.

An overloaded function has multiple arrow types in its function type,
and it associates a declaration with each constituent arrow type.
When an overloaded function of type \VAR{T} is called with an argument of type
\VAR{A}, the call is ``dispatched'' to the declaration associated with
the most specific type of \VAR{T} applicable to \VAR{A}
(if no such type exists, then the function is not applicable to \VAR{A}).
This is well defined because the overloading rules guarantee that
the type of any function value is a well-formed function type.

If a function's argument type is \EXP{()},
then function declarations with the following forms of parameter lists are
considered to be applicable:
\begin{itemize}
\item   \EXP{()}
which means the same thing as \EXP{(\_\COLONOP())}
\item   \EXP{(x\COLONOP())}
which is something programmers don't ordinarily write
\item   \EXP{(x\COLONOP{}T\ldots)}
\end{itemize}
In the last case, \VAR{x} is bound to an empty
\EXP{\TYP{HeapSequence}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}.

If a function's argument type \VAR{A} is
    neither \EXP{()} nor a tuple type, then function declarations with the following forms of parameter lists are considered
    to be applicable:
\begin{itemize}
\item
        \EXP{(x\COLONOP{}T)}       where \VAR{A} is a subtype of \VAR{T}
\item
        \EXP{(x\COLONOP{}T\ldots)} where \VAR{A} is a subtype of \VAR{T}
\end{itemize}
In the last case, \VAR{x} is bound to a
    \EXP{\TYP{HeapSequence}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} of length \EXP{1},
    containing  the actual argument value.

If a function's argument type \VAR{A} is
a tuple type, then function declarations with the following forms of
parameter lists are considered to be applicable:
\begin{itemize}
\item
        \EXP{(x\COLONOP{}T)}       where \VAR{A} is a subtype of \VAR{T}
\item
        \EXP{(x\COLONOP{}T\ldots)} where \VAR{A} is a subtype of \VAR{T}
\item
a parameter list with no varargs binding, provided that
 \begin{itemize}
 \item type \VAR{A} has exactly as many plain types as the parameter
list has plain bindings, and
 \item for every keyword-type pair (described in
\secref{tuple-types}) in \VAR{A}, the parameter list has a
binding with the same keyword, and
 \item for every element type in \VAR{A}, the type in the element type
is a subtype of the type of the corresponding binding in the parameter list.
 \end{itemize}
\item
a parameter list with a varargs binding, provided that
 \begin{itemize}
 \item type \VAR{A} has at least as many plain types as the parameter
list has plain bindings, and
 \item for every keyword-type pair in
\VAR{A}, the parameter list has a binding with the same keyword, and
 \item for every element type in \VAR{A}, the type in the element type
is a subtype of the type of the corresponding binding in the parameter
list---but if there is no corresponding binding, then the type in the
element type must be a subtype of the type in the varargs binding.
 \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
    In the latter case, the parameter named by the identifier in the varargs
    binding is bound to a \EXP{\TYP{HeapSequence}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
    that contains, in order, all the
 values of the tuple that did not correspond to plain
    bindings, followed by all the values in the varargs \TYP{HeapSequence}
    of the tuple, if any.

When an argument is passed explicitly for a keyword parameter, that
argument must be passed as a \emph{keyword argument}.
Syntactically, a keyword argument is a keyword-value pair
``\EXP{\VAR{identifier} = e}''.
Keyword parameters not explicitly bound are bound to their default values.
If a parameter that has no default value is not explicitly bound to an
argument, it is a static error.

When a function is called (See \secref{function-calls} for a discussion
of function call expressions), function arguments are evaluated in parallel,
keyword parameters not explicitly bound are bound to their
default values sequentially,
and the body of the function is evaluated in
a new environment, extending the environment in which
it is defined with all parameters bound to their arguments.

If the application of a function \VAR{f} ends by calling another
function \VAR{g}, tail-call
optimization must be applied.  Storage used by the new environments
constructed for the application of \VAR{f} must be reclaimed.

== Specification/basic/overloading.tex:246-287

\section{Applicability for Functionals with Varargs and Keyword Parameters}
\seclabel{applicability-with-special-params}

The basic idea for handling varargs and keyword
parameters is that we
can think of a functional declaration that has such parameters as
though it were (possibly infinitely) many declarations, one for each
set of arguments it may be called with.  In other words, we expand
these declarations so that there exists a declaration for each number
of arguments that can be passed to it.


A declaration with a varargs parameter corresponds to an infinite
number of declarations, one for every number of arguments that may be
passed to the varargs parameter.  In practice, we can bound that
number by the maximum number of arguments that the functional is
called with anywhere in the program (in other words, a given program
will contain only a finite number of calls with different numbers of
arguments).  The expansion described here is a conceptual one to
simplify the description of the semantics; we do not expect a real
implementation to actually expand these declarations at compile time.
%
For example, the following declaration:
%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ, z : ZZ...):ZZ
\begin{Fortress}
\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}\ldots)\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)
\end{Fortress}
would be expanded into:
%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ):ZZ
%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ, z1 : ZZ):ZZ
%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ, z1 : ZZ, z2 : ZZ):ZZ
%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ, z1 : ZZ, z2 : ZZ, z3 : ZZ):ZZ
%...
\begin{Fortress}
\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{2} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{2} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{3} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
\(\ldots\)
\end{Fortress}
A declaration with a varargs parameter is applicable to a call if
any one of the expanded declarations is applicable.

# Rung G, climb batch 33b: record lines

## Findings

1. **The code generator compiles a varargs parameter against the one library as one immutable array of the arguments that no plain parameter takes.** Conditions: under `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, or wherever the compile command's names point to `FortressLibrary`; a declaration at top level, in a trait or object, or local to a block, and an operator. The varargs part of a domain is one JVM parameter of `ImmutableArray[\T, ZZ32\]` of the library in use, after the plain parameters (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/NamingCzar.java:945-968`); the caller makes the array with the library's `__immutableFactory1[\T, 0, k\]()` and puts each further argument at its index with `init`, in order (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:7695-7831`). Evidence: `one_library_tests/OneLibraryVarargsCount.test`, `OneLibraryVarargsMethod.test`, `OneLibraryVarargsOperator.test`, `OneLibraryVarargsLocalFunction.test`, each failing on the base ('Can't compile VarArgs yet', `OptionUnwrapException`, 'Index 0 out of bounds for length 0') and passing on `4526151e00` (`OK (6 tests)` with the run test); the bytecode of `count(4, 5, 6)` in `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-varargs/REPORT.md`, "The convention as built". Meaning: row 624 closes under the selector; `println`'s path through `WriteStream` compiles.
2. **Where another declaration of the name takes as many arguments, the call goes to the dispatch method of that arity, whose branch for the varargs declaration makes the array.** Conditions: a top-level function or operator without static parameters; the dispatch methods hold the varargs declaration at each number of arguments from its plain count to the most another member takes (`CodeGen.java:8514-8541`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:187-244`, `:2024-2033`); beyond, and for a generic declaration, the call makes the array. Evidence: `one_library_tests/OneLibraryVarargsOverloaded.test`: `check(z, z)` calls the dispatch method `check(Any;Any)`, `check(z, z, "a")` makes an array of one; the library's `assert(z, z)` calls `FortressLibrary.assert(Any;Any)`. Meaning: the expansion rule of `Specification/basic/overloading.tex`, "Applicability for Functionals with Varargs and Keyword Parameters", is how the compiled dispatch reads a varargs declaration.
3. **Against the compiler's prelude the code generator refuses a varargs declaration, naming the missing array type.** 'Can't compile VarArgs yet: the library in use, CompilerLibrary, declares no ImmutableArray, the type of a varargs parameter' (`NamingCzar.java:945-951`). Evidence: `compiler_tests/XXXVarargsCodeGeneration.test` (unchanged) and `XXXVarargsMethodCodeGeneration.test` (its message, from `OptionUnwrapException`), both expected failures on `4526151e00`. Meaning: P-37 holds; row 604's checker refusals stand beside it.
4. **On the code of `888c20dd93`, the planner's measure finds 3 refused declarations of the fourteen components, 751 emitted, in 2 kinds; the ten of varargs are emitted, `Generator2` and `CatString` among them.** Command: `explorations/compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/planner/codegen-measure.sh <scratch-worktree> <out-dir>`; output 'refused declarations 3 | emitted (OK lines) 751 | component failures 0', the closure class twice (row 315) and `__bigOperator2` (row 1076). Meaning: F-34's count of 13 on `d3747846c1` falls by the ten of row 624; nothing stands behind varargs in those ten. The measure skips the dispatch methods.
5. **A spread argument to a varargs parameter, `f(1, ys...)`, is dropped on both paths.** The parser keeps it (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/DelimitedExpr.rats:180-186`); walk evaluates only the argument tuple's plain elements (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:1471-1473`); the compiled checker's `getArgList` takes only them (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:87`), so the compiled call has none. Evidence: `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXVarargsSpreadArgument.fss`, 'FAIL: a ZZ32: 1 =/= a ZZ32: 3' under `harness-one.sh`, an expected failure; compiled under the selection, `count(1, ys...)` makes an array of one. Meaning: NEW-G-1; the specification's examples `f(1, [2 3]...)` do not run on either path.
6. **The code generator makes the one library's `ZZ32` from a JVM int as `FZZ32.make`, where the one library's descriptors name `fortress/FortressLibrary$ZZ32`.** Conditions: under the selection; the varargs array's indices (`CodeGen.java:7823-7825`), as `forIntLiteralExpr` (`CodeGen.java:4636-4642`) and the numeral sites (`FZZ.make` values passed to `coerce_ZZ32?natural`, whose descriptor names `fortress/FortressLibrary$ZZ`). Evidence: `javap -c -p` of `OneLibraryVarargsCount$task0` (`invokestatic FZZ32.make` before `init:(Lfortress/FortressLibrary$ZZ32;...)`). Meaning: no program runs on the one library until its numbers have their carriers (fork N4); a note on row 1062.

## For FACTS

**The code generator passes a varargs parameter's arguments as one `ImmutableArray[\T, ZZ32\]` of the library in use, made at the call or in a dispatch method's branch.** The varargs part of a domain is one JVM parameter after the plain ones; the array is made by `__immutableFactory1` and filled in order with `init`, as walk makes it; a call goes to the dispatch method of its arity where another declaration of the name takes as many arguments, by the expansion rule.
